SOURCE: Learning Performance-Improving Code Edits. Shypula, Madaan, Zeng, Alon, Gardner, Hashemi, Neubig, Ranganathan, Bastani, Yazdanbakhsh. ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2302.07867v5, 26 Apr 2024).

COVERAGE: I read all 25 of 25 pages (68,725 of 68,725 chars), including Appendices A.1–A.11 (pp. 14–25). I only skimmed the references (pp. 10–13) to trace where the method comes from.

CLAIMS (most important first)

- claim: On real hardware, timing two identical programs against each other produces fake speedups. This is the paper's reason for using a simulator.
  number: mean 1.12×, sd 0.36, top 5% at 1.91×
  setup: The authors used hyperfine (a Rust benchmarking tool) on 500 pairs where the "slow" and "fast" programs were the same program, so the true ratio is 1.
  quote: "We benchmarked 500 programs “pairs” where the “slow” and “fast” programs are identical. Ideally, we should have source time/target time = 1 ... However, we observed a mean speedup of 1.12 ×, with a standard deviation of 0.36, and the top 5% of pairs exhibited a speedup of 1.91×."
  where: pp. 3–4

- claim: All runtimes are measured in the gem5 full-system simulator. A deterministic program gives the same timing on every run, so the measurement is reproducible.
  number: none
  setup: gem5 "Verbatim configuration of the Intel Skylake architecture", GCC 9.3.0, C++17, -O3. Any gain is therefore on top of what the optimizing compiler already does. The two-minute timeout is the one source of variability the authors admit.
  quote: "Executing deterministic programs in gem5 provides deterministic performance results. This enables reproducibility in research and denoised performance measurements." Footnote 2: "This assumes gem5 terminates. Our experiments use a two-minute timeout, which may introduce slight variability. Note that altering this timeout could change the results."
  where: p. 4; compiler settings on p. 6

- claim: CodeNet's own CPU-time labels cannot be trusted, so every program was re-timed in gem5.
  number: 2.44×; 42.8 million simulations
  setup: Two identical template-code submissions to problem p03160 had different CodeNet runtimes.
  quote: "a speedup of 2.44× is reported, despite the programs and environments being identical." / "to create these annotated runtimes, we performed over 42.8 million simulations in our gem5 environment."
  where: p. 21 (A.9); p. 3

- claim: Correctness means passing every test, and one failure rejects the program. CodeNet's roughly 4 tests per problem were supplemented with tests generated by AlphaCode's LLM.
  number: about 4 tests per problem in CodeNet; median 82.5 (train), 75 (val), 104 (test) after adding tests
  setup: Tests whose gem5 run took over 2 minutes were dropped.
  quote: "we reject the program if a single test fails. CodeNet includes an average of 4 test cases per problem. To improve coverage, we include additional test cases from AlphaCode (Li et al., 2022) generated with a fine-tuned LLM. A small set of test cases would lead to substantial timeouts above 2 minutes in gem5; after excluding them, we obtain a median of 82.5 test cases per problem in our training set, 75 test cases per problem in our validation set, and 104 test cases per problem for our test set"
  where: p. 3

- claim: Even with the added tests, some speedups were spurious. The tests did not exercise large inputs, so a model could shrink array allocations and still pass. The paper gives no formal false-positive rate; this manual audit is the closest figure.
  number: 10 of 120
  setup: The authors manually inspected 120 random (source, optimized) pairs from GPT-3.5 fine-tuned with HQ data plus self-play.
  quote: "in 10 out of the 120 cases we examined, the speedup stemmed from reducing the constants used to allocate arrays. These speedups might not always reflect genuine algorithmic improvements, and indicate that the test cases may not perfectly cover all the cases, an open problem in code synthesis"
  where: p. 14

- claim: How the dataset was built. The authors took one user's chronological accepted CodeNet C++ submissions to a problem, formed every earlier→later pair, and kept pairs with a relative time gain above 10%. Splits are by problem, so no problem appears in two splits.
  number: 77,967 train pairs from 1,474 problems; 2,544 val pairs from 77 problems; 978 test pairs from 41 problems
  setup: Only accepted submissions were used; programs that failed tests or timed out were removed first.
  quote: "We obtain a training set of 77,967 pairs from 1,474 problems, a validation set of 2,544 pairs from 77 problems, and a test set of 978 pairs from 41 problems."
  where: p. 3

- claim: Metric definitions. Any generation that is incorrect or slower counts as a speedup of 1.0, so a failure is never rewarded. %Opt needs both correctness and at least a 10% gain.
  number: 10%; 1.0
  setup: Best@k means the fastest of k samples that passes all tests, sampled at temperature 0.7.
  quote: "Percent Optimized [%OPT]: The fraction of programs in the test set (out of 978 unseen samples) improved by a certain method. A program must be at least 10% faster and correct to contribute." / "For generations that are either incorrect or slower than the original program, we use a speedup of 1.0 for that example" / "We use BEST @k to denote this strategy with k samples and a temperature of 0.7."
  where: p. 6
  Speedup is defined as old time divided by new time and averaged over all test examples. %Correct is reported only as a "secondary outcome".

- claim: The best model beats the average human edit at Best@8. The table also shows Speedup and %Correct moving independently of each other.
  number: Human reference 3.66×. GPT-3.5 fine-tuned with self-play: 87.63% %Opt, 6.86×, 95.09% correct. CodeLlama 13B perf-conditioned: 66.56%, 5.65×, 70.96%. GPT-4 with retrieval: 76.07%, 3.93×, 95.71%. GPT-3.5 with CoT: 43.05%, 1.60×, 91.72%.
  setup: Table 1, Best@8, 978-pair test set.
  quote: "Human reference 100.00% 3.66× 100.00%" ... "FineTune (P) GPT-3.5, Self-Play 87.63% 6.86× 95.09%"
  where: p. 6, Table 1

- claim: At a larger sampling budget, the model's fastest generation slightly beats the fastest human submission for each problem.
  number: 9.64× vs 9.56×
  setup: 39,129 model generations (40 samples) compared with 118,841 accepted human solutions.
  quote: "For the PIE dataset, the best human speedup achieved was 9.56×, while our model achieved a slightly higher speedup of 9.64×, setting a new upper limit."
  where: p. 8

- claim: Prompting without PIE data does little. Few-shot examples were often no better than the instruction alone.
  number: CodeLlama 7B instruction-only: 1.01× and 23.52% correct at Best@1
  setup: Table 2.
  quote: "Instruction-Only CODELLAMA 7B 0.92% 1.01 × 23.52%"
  where: p. 7

- claim: Error analysis of the best model's failures shows most of them break a test. Speed-only failures still make up about 30%.
  number: 12.51% failed to compile; 27.59% got 95–100% of tests wrong; 9.93% slower than the original; 10.75% faster but below 1.1×
  setup: Table 5, GPT-3.5 fine-tuned with self-play.
  quote: "Ran all test cases, the program was faster, but not 1.1× speedup or higher 10.75%"
  where: p. 18

- claim: The paper never runs a held-out sampling diversity test. It does, however, report that performance-conditioning lowers correctness.
  number: 59.95% → 64.36% %Correct
  setup: Six generations from the CodeLlama 7B perf-conditioned model all tagged 10/10, compared with six generations spread across the 10/10, 9/10 and 8/10 tags.
  quote: "we saw a %Correct increase from 59.95% to 64.36%."
  where: p. 18

- claim: LoRA fine-tuning hardly helps.
  number: about 1.15–1.17× at Best@8
  setup: Table 10, rank 32, alpha 16.
  quote: "All CODELLAMA 7B 1.12% 1.01 × 45.82% 9.57% 1.17× 87.47%"
  where: p. 22

LIMITS
- Correctness depends only on tests. The authors concede that the tests "may not perfectly cover all the cases" (10 of 120 audited speedups were spurious). There is no formal false-positive rate, and they did not audit the human or other-model results.
- gem5 removes noise, but only for one simulated Skylake configuration. The paper does not show that simulated speedups match real-hardware speedups. The two-minute timeout can change results (footnote 2), and tests that ran longer were dropped, which biases the test set toward shorter runs.
- Only C++ competitive-programming solutions are covered, with a test set of 41 problems. The paper reports no confidence intervals or seeds for any metric.
- Speedup is averaged with failures counted as 1.0, so a high mean can hide a low %Correct. For example, CodeLlama 13B perf-conditioned reaches 5.65× with only 70.96% correct.
- The models have dated: gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 and gpt-4-0613 (GPT-4 could not be fine-tuned at the time), and CodeLlama base models.
- There are internal inconsistencies, listed under PROBLEMS.

BUILDS ON: CodeNet (Puri et al., 2021) for the source programs; the gem5 simulator (Binkert et al., 2011) with a Skylake configuration (github darchr/gem5-skylake-config); AlphaCode's generated tests and the best-of-k sampling idea (Li et al., 2022); hyperfine (Peter, 2023) for the noise demonstration; CoT (Wei et al., 2022b); retrieval-based prompting (Liu et al., 2021; Poesia et al., 2021), using CodeBERTScore (Zhou et al., 2023b) and FAISS (Johnson et al., 2019); self-play (Haluptzok et al., 2022); performance-conditioning modelled on Decision Transformer (Chen et al., 2021a) and Zhang et al. (2023); the "small high-quality data" idea from LIMA (Zhou et al., 2023a) and AlpaGasus (Chen et al., 2023). Earlier performance work it cites: DeepPERF (Garg et al., 2022) and Chen et al. (2022).

CODE: The performance-conditioned inference prompt (Figure 2, p. 5), verbatim:
```
This is a slow program we want
to optimize to score 10/10.
### Program:
{src_code}
### Optimized Version:
```
The dataset pair filter (p. 3): keep a pair when (time(yi) − time(y>i)) / time(yi) > 10%.

FIGURES
- Table 1, p. 6: "Summary of Results: This table reports our strongest performing models by SPEEDUP across different adaptation regimes". It puts %Opt, Speedup and %Correct side by side against the human reference, so a reader can see that the three metrics disagree. This is the best candidate for an eval note.
- Figure 1, p. 2: "An example of a program that solves the problem of “compute the sum of the numbers from 1 to N”. The program on the left runs in O(N), whereas the program on the right runs in constant time." It explains the task in one glance.
- Figures 8/9, p. 17: "%Opt / Speedup over generations comparison of GPT-3.5 fine-tuned with HQ Data Only vs. HQ + Self-Play". These show how Best@k grows as k goes from 1 to 8.
- The hyperfine 1.12×/1.91× result is prose only, with no figure.

PROBLEMS
- The text extraction cut off C++ printf/scanf format strings at "%" in Figures 3–7, 11 and 17. Fig. 11 also loses a "||". Images were not extracted. I did not run figures.py; the captions above come from the text.
- The paper contradicts itself. Section 4.3 (p. 9) says retrieval lifted CodeLlama 34B "to 34.25% %OPT, 2.28× SPEEDUP for BEST@8", but Table 3 (K=4) gives 42.54% and 2.43×. The 34.25%/2.28× figures match the K=2 row of Table 9. Separately, A.3 (p. 17) says "speedup and correctness increase from 6.74 → 6.86 and 86.71 → 87.63", but 86.71→87.63 is %Opt, not correctness; %Correct actually fell from 95.40 to 95.09.
- Section 4.1 (p. 7) says retrieval results are in "Table 2 (bottom)", but they are in Table 3.
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
